Qatada said: he was called "possessor of stakes" because he had canopies, playgrounds and stakes to which he was tied, and they played beneath them. Muhammad ibn Kaʿb said: it means possessor of firm construction. Saʿid ibn Jubayr said: he had minarets on which he tortured people. Mujahid and others said: he tortured people with stakes; when he became angry with someone he would stretch him on the ground and stake his hands, feet and head to the ground.

Ibn Fanjawayh informed me, saying: Mukhallad related to us, saying: Ibn ʿAlawiyya related to us, saying: Ismaʿil related to us, saying: Ishaq ibn Bishr related to us from Ibn Sam'an, from ʿAta', from Ibn ʿAbbas, that when Pharaoh was told "possessor of stakes," [it was] that she was a woman, namely the woman of his treasurer Kharbil,[[Al-Qurtubi in his tafsir (15/306) cited from al-Tha'labi that his name was Hizqil.]] son of Nuhabil, and he was a believer who concealed his faith for a hundred years,[[As mentioned in Taj al-Arus (7/302); it was also said six hundred years, mentioned by al-Jaza'iri in al-Qisas: 253.]] and he had met some of the companions of Joseph; and his wife was the hairdresser of Pharaoh's daughter. One day, while she was combing the head of Pharaoh's daughter, the comb fell from her hand, and she said: "Woe to the one who disbelieves in God." Pharaoh's daughter said: "Do you have a god other than my father?" She said: "My God and your father's God and the God of the heavens and the earth is one, without partner."

She got up, entered upon her father weeping. He said: "What makes you weep?" She said: "The hairdresser, the woman of your treasurer, claims that your god and her god and the god of the heavens and the earth is one, without partner." He sent for her and asked her about that, and she said: "You have spoken the truth." He said to her: "Woe to you! Disbelieve in your god and affirm that I am your god." She said: "I will not do that." So he stretched her between four stakes, then sent upon her snakes and scorpions, and said to her: "Disbelieve in God, or I will torture you with this torment for two months." She said: "By God, if you tortured me for seventy months I would not disbelieve in God, the Exalted."

He said: She had two daughters, so he brought the elder daughter and slaughtered her in front of her mouth, and said to her: "Disbelieve in God, or I will slaughter your younger daughter in front of your mouth." The younger was a nursing infant, and she felt a great pang for her. She said: "Even if you slaughtered whoever is on the earth in front of my mouth, I would not disbelieve in God, the Exalted."

He said: He brought the daughter, and when she was brought forward, laid down upon her chest and they were about to slaughter her, the mother became distressed. God loosened the tongue of her daughter, and she spoke, for she was one of the four who spoke while infants. She said: "O mother, do not be distressed, for God has built for you a house in Paradise. Be patient, for you are going to the mercy and honor of God." He said: She was slaughtered, and she had not lingered before she died, and God settled her in Paradise.

He said: He sent to seek her husband Kharbil, but they could not find him. It was said to Pharaoh: "He has been seen in such and such a place, in such and such mountains." He sent two men in pursuit of him, and they reached him while he was praying, and three rows of wild beasts were behind him praying. When they saw that, they turned back. Kharbil said: "O God, You know that I concealed my faith for a hundred years, and no one discovered me. Of these two men, whichever concealed [my whereabouts] from me, guide him to Your religion and give him from the world what he asks; and of these two men, whichever revealed me, hasten his punishment in this world, and make his final destination the Fire." The two men returned to Pharaoh. One of them took heed and believed, while the other informed Pharaoh of the story before the chiefs. Pharaoh said to him: "Was there anyone with you other than yourself?" He said: "Yes."

He said: "And who was with you?" He said: "So-and-so." He summoned him. He said: "Is what this one says true?" He said: "No, I did not see anything of what he said." Pharaoh gave him and rewarded him generously. As for the other, he killed him and then crucified him.

He said: Pharaoh had married a woman, one of the most beautiful women of the Children of Israel, called Asiya daughter of Muzahim. When she saw what Pharaoh had done to the hairdresser, she said: "How could I bear to be patient with what Pharaoh has done, while I am a Muslim and he is a disbeliever?" While she was thus deliberating within herself, Pharaoh entered upon her and sat near her. She said: "O Pharaoh, you are the worst and most vile of creatures. You went to the hairdresser and killed her." He said: "Perhaps the madness that afflicted her has also afflicted you."

She said: "I have no madness. My God and your God and the God of the heavens and the earth is one, without partner." He tore at her and beat her, and sent for her parents, summoned them, and told them the matter, that the madness which had afflicted the hairdresser had afflicted her. She said: "I seek refuge in God from that. I testify that my Lord and your Lord and the Lord of the heavens and the earth is one, without partner." Her father said: "O Asiya, are you not the best of the women of the Amalekites, and your husband the god of the Amalekites?" She said: "I seek refuge in God from that, if what you say is true. So tell him: let him crown me with a crown, with the sun in front of it, the moon behind it, and the stars around it." Pharaoh said to them: "Get out of my presence." Abu Jaʿfar, Abu Hatim and Warsh pronounced the ya' in "al-wad" when pausing and continuing, Ibn Kathir in the narration of al-Bazzi and al-ʿAwwas and Yaʿqub kept it according to the original, while the others omitted it in both situations because it is the end of a verse.

﴿And Pharaoh, possessor of stakes﴾. They differed concerning it. Some said: it means possessor of hosts and armies who strengthened his command and secured his kingdom, and the soldiers were called "stakes" because of the many tents they pitched and fixed on their journeys. This is the narration of ʿAtiyya from Ibn ʿAbbas.

Qatada said: he was called "possessor of stakes" because he had canopies, playgrounds and stakes to which he was tied, and they played beneath them. Muhammad ibn Kaʿb said: it means possessor of firm construction. Saʿid ibn Jubayr said: he had minarets on which he tortured people. Mujahid and others said: he tortured people with stakes; when he became angry with someone he would stretch him on the ground and stake his hands, feet and head to the ground.

Ibn Fanjawayh informed me, saying: Mukhallad related to us, saying: Ibn ʿAlawiyya related to us, saying: Ismaʿil related to us, saying: Ishaq ibn Bishr related to us from Ibn Sam'an, from ʿAta', from Ibn ʿAbbas, that when Pharaoh was told "possessor of stakes," [it was] that she was a woman, namely the woman of his treasurer Kharbil,[[Al-Qurtubi in his tafsir (15/306) cited from al-Tha'labi that his name was Hizqil.]] son of Nuhabil, and he was a believer who concealed his faith for a hundred years,[[As mentioned in Taj al-Arus (7/302); it was also said six hundred years, mentioned by al-Jaza'iri in al-Qisas: 253.]] and he had met some of the companions of Joseph; and his wife was the hairdresser of Pharaoh's daughter. One day, while she was combing the head of Pharaoh's daughter, the comb fell from her hand, and she said: "Woe to the one who disbelieves in God." Pharaoh's daughter said: "Do you have a god other than my father?" She said: "My God and your father's God and the God of the heavens and the earth is one, without partner."

She got up, entered upon her father weeping. He said: "What makes you weep?" She said: "The hairdresser, the woman of your treasurer, claims that your god and her god and the god of the heavens and the earth is one, without partner." He sent for her and asked her about that, and she said: "You have spoken the truth." He said to her: "Woe to you! Disbelieve in your god and affirm that I am your god." She said: "I will not do that." So he stretched her between four stakes, then sent upon her snakes and scorpions, and said to her: "Disbelieve in God, or I will torture you with this torment for two months." She said: "By God, if you tortured me for seventy months I would not disbelieve in God, the Exalted."

He said: She had two daughters, so he brought the elder daughter and slaughtered her in front of her mouth, and said to her: "Disbelieve in God, or I will slaughter your younger daughter in front of your mouth." The younger was a nursing infant, and she felt a great pang for her. She said: "Even if you slaughtered whoever is on the earth in front of my mouth, I would not disbelieve in God, the Exalted."

He said: He brought the daughter, and when she was brought forward, laid down upon her chest and they were about to slaughter her, the mother became distressed. God loosened the tongue of her daughter, and she spoke, for she was one of the four who spoke while infants. She said: "O mother, do not be distressed, for God has built for you a house in Paradise. Be patient, for you are going to the mercy and honor of God." He said: She was slaughtered, and she had not lingered before she died, and God settled her in Paradise.

He said: He sent to seek her husband Kharbil, but they could not find him. It was said to Pharaoh: "He has been seen in such and such a place, in such and such mountains." He sent two men in pursuit of him, and they reached him while he was praying, and three rows of wild beasts were behind him praying. When they saw that, they turned back. Kharbil said: "O God, You know that I concealed my faith for a hundred years, and no one discovered me. Of these two men, whichever concealed [my whereabouts] from me, guide him to Your religion and give him from the world what he asks; and of these two men, whichever revealed me, hasten his punishment in this world, and make his final destination the Fire." The two men returned to Pharaoh. One of them took heed and believed, while the other informed Pharaoh of the story before the chiefs. Pharaoh said to him: "Was there anyone with you other than yourself?" He said: "Yes."

He said: "And who was with you?" He said: "So-and-so." He summoned him. He said: "Is what this one says true?" He said: "No, I did not see anything of what he said." Pharaoh gave him and rewarded him generously. As for the other, he killed him and then crucified him.

He said: Pharaoh had married a woman, one of the most beautiful women of the Children of Israel, called Asiya daughter of Muzahim. When she saw what Pharaoh had done to the hairdresser, she said: "How could I bear to be patient with what Pharaoh has done, while I am a Muslim and he is a disbeliever?" While she was thus deliberating within herself, Pharaoh entered upon her and sat near her. She said: "O Pharaoh, you are the worst and most vile of creatures. You went to the hairdresser and killed her." He said: "Perhaps the madness that afflicted her has also afflicted you."

She said: "I have no madness. My God and your God and the God of the heavens and the earth is one, without partner." He tore at her and beat her, and sent for her parents, summoned them, and told them the matter, that the madness which had afflicted the hairdresser had afflicted her. She said: "I seek refuge in God from that. I testify that my Lord and your Lord and the Lord of the heavens and the earth is one, without partner." Her father said: "O Asiya, are you not the best of the women of the Amalekites, and your husband the god of the Amalekites?" She said: "I seek refuge in God from that, if what you say is true. So tell him: let him crown me with a crown, with the sun in front of it, the moon behind it, and the stars around it." Pharaoh said to them: "Get out of my presence." He stretched her between four stakes to torture her. God opened for her a gate to Paradise to make easier for her what Pharaoh did to her. At that moment she said: ﴿My Lord, build for me near You a house in Paradise, and save me from Pharaoh and his deeds﴾, meaning from Pharaoh's intercourse, ﴿and save me from the wrongdoing people﴾, meaning from Pharaoh and his party. God took her soul and settled her in Paradise.[[The story with variations in the long narrations of al-Tabarani: 115; Tafsir Ibn Kathir: 4/420.]]

It was also said: the stakes are a metaphor for the stability of his kingdom, the length of his reign and the severity of his majesty, like the firmness of stakes in the earth, as the poet al-Aswad said:

﴿In the shade of a king of firm stakes﴾.[[Maʿani al-Qur'an by al-Nahhas: 6/85; Muʿjam al-Buldan: 1/272, whose opening line is: "And they indeed delighted therein in the finest living."]]

﴿Who transgressed in the lands and multiplied corruption therein, so your Lord poured upon them a scourge of punishment.﴾ Qatada said: it means a kind of punishment He poured upon them. Al-Suddi said: every day a different kind of punishment. It was also said: the pain of punishment. The people of the meanings said: this is figurative, because the whip, in their view, is the extreme of punishment, so it applies to every punishment. The poet said:

﴿Do you not see that God has made His religion manifest, and poured upon the disbelievers a whip of punishment?﴾

﴿Indeed your Lord is in the watchtower.﴾ Ibn ʿAbbas said: He, glory be to Him, sees and hears. Muqatil said: He watches over people on the Sirat (bridge), so He placed a watch of angels with them, carrying hooks, staves and thorns. Al-Dahhak said: in a watchtower over the people of wrongdoing and disobedience. It was also said: its meaning is that the return of creation and their destination is to His judgment and command. Al-Hasan and ʿIkrima said: He watches the deeds of the children of Adam. Also from Muqatil: their passing by it. ʿAta' ibn Abi Rabah: no one escapes Him. Yaman: there is no escape from Him. Al-Suddi: He sets the Fire on their paths until it destroys them. The word "al-mirsad" and "al-marsad" mean the path, and the plural of "al-mirsad" is "marasid," and the plural of "al-marsad" is "marasid."

Muqsim narrated from Ibn ʿAbbas, who said: Over Hell there are seven checkpoints. The servants are questioned at the first of them about the testimony that there is no god but God. If he brings it complete, he passes to the second, where he is asked about prayer. If he brings it complete, he passes to the third, where he is asked about zakat. If he brings it complete, he passes to the fourth, where he is asked about fasting. If he brings it complete, he passes to the fifth, where he is asked about Hajj. If he brings it complete, he passes to the sixth, where he is asked about 'Umra. If he brings it complete, he passes to the seventh, where he is asked about wrongful acts. If he is clear of them, well; otherwise it is said, "Wait and see." If he has voluntary acts, they complete his deeds, and when he has finished with them he is taken to Paradise.

He said: "Arama banu fulan," meaning they were destroyed. This is also the narration of al-ʿAwfi from Ibn ʿAbbas.

It is also narrated from al-Dahhak that he recited ﴿Iram of the pillars﴾, meaning: He destroyed them and made them crumbled bones (rumim). The correct view is that it is the name of a tribe or a town, and therefore it is not inflected (with kasra).[[Tafsir al-Tabari: 30/220.]]

As for His words ﴿of the pillars﴾, a group said: it means possessors of height, strength and might.

Ibn Fanjawayh informed me, saying: Ibn Hanash related to us, saying: Abu al-Qasim ibn al-Fadl related to us, saying: Abu Hatim related to us, saying: Abu Salih, the scribe of al-Layth, related to us, saying: Muʿawiya ibn Salih related to me from one who related to him, from al-Miqdam, from the Prophet (ﷺ), that he mentioned ﴿Iram of the pillars﴾ and said: "A man among them would come with a rock, carry it on his shoulder, and throw it upon whatever tribe he wished, destroying them."[144][[Tafsir al-Durr al-Manthur: 6/347; Fath al-Bari: 8/538.]]

Al-Kalbi said: the height of a man among them was four hundred cubits. Ibn ʿAbbas said: it means their height was like pillars, and the Arabs call a tall man "muʿammad." Muqatil said: the height of one of them was twelve cubits. Others said: they were only called "of the pillars" because they were people of mobile pillars (tents), who followed the rain and moved to pasture wherever it was, and then returned to their dwellings and did not stay in one place.

Al-Kalbi said: Iram is the one to whom the lineage of ʿAd, Thamud, the people of the Sawad and the people of al-Jazira converge. It used to be said: "ʿAd Iram and Thamud Iram." Then God destroyed ʿAd, then Thamud, and the people of the Sawad and al-Jazira remained. They were people of pillars, tents and livestock in spring, and when the grass withered they returned to their dwellings; they were people of gardens and crops, and their dwellings were in Wadi al-Qura, which is the one of which God says: ﴿the like of which was not created in the lands﴾.

It was also said: they were named "of the pillars" because of a building one of them built, whose pillars he reinforced and whose structure he raised. ʿImad, ʿumud and ʿumud are plurals of ʿamud (pillar).

What Abu al-Qasim the exegete informed us, saying: Abu ʿAbdullah Muhammad ibn ʿAbdullah ibn Ahmad al-Saffar al-Isfahani informed us, saying: Abu Jaʿfar Ahmad ibn Mahdi ibn Rustam al-Isfahani informed us, saying: ʿAbdullah ibn Salih al-Misri related to us, saying: Ibn Lahiʿa related to me. And Abu al-Qasim informed us, saying: Abu al-Hasan Ahmad ibn Muhammad ibn ʿAbdus al-Taraʾifi informed us, saying: ʿUthman ibn Saʿid al-Darji informed us, saying: ʿAbdullah ibn Salih related to us, saying: Ibn Lahiʿa related to me from Khalid ibn Abi ʿImran, from Wahb ibn Munabbih, from ʿAbdullah ibn Qilaba, that he went out seeking camels of his that had strayed. While he was in the deserts of Aden, he came upon a city in those wastelands, with a fortress upon which were great palaces and tall pillars. When he drew near, he thought there was someone there he could ask about his camels, but he saw no one going out or coming in. He dismounted, tethered his mount, drew his sword and entered through the gate of the fortress. When he entered the fortress, he found two enormous gates, larger than any he had seen, both inlaid with white and red rubies. When he saw this he was astonished and amazed, and he opened one of the gates, and there was a city the like of which no one had seen. Each palace had pillars of chrysolite and ruby hanging beneath it, and above each palace were upper chambers:

[Take heed, O you deceived by a long life... I am Shaddad ibn ʿAd, owner of the lofty fortress,
and brother of might and hardship and the gathered kingdom... the abode of the people of the earth fears my threat and warning,
and I ruled East and West with a mighty authority... and by the bounty of kingship, its troops and its multitude,
Then Hud came, and we were in error before Hud... he called us, had we accepted him, to the right course,
but we disobeyed him and cried out, "Is there any escape?" Then a cry came upon us, descending from the distant horizon,
so we were gathered like crops cut down in a wide wilderness.]

One day, while she was combing the head of Pharaoh's daughter, the comb fell from her hand, and she said: "Woe to the one who disbelieves in God." Pharaoh's daughter said: "Do you have a god other than my father?" She said: "My God and your father's God and the God of the heavens and the earth is one, without partner."

Ibn Fanjawayh informed us, saying: Ibn Hanash related to us, saying: Abu al-Tayyib al-Marwazi related to us, saying: Muhammad ibn ʿAli related to us, saying: Fadl ibn Khalid informed us, saying: ʿUbayd ibn Sulayman related to us from al-Dahhak ibn Muzahim that he used to recite ﴿Iram of the pillars﴾ with a fatha on the alif and the ra', and that Iram means destruction. He said: "Arama banu fulan," meaning they were destroyed. This is also the narration of al-ʿAwfi from Ibn ʿAbbas.

It is also narrated from al-Dahhak that he recited ﴿Iram of the pillars﴾, meaning: He destroyed them and made them crumbled bones (rumim). The correct view is that it is the name of a tribe or a town, and therefore it is not inflected (with kasra).[[Tafsir al-Tabari: 30/220.]]

As for His words ﴿of the pillars﴾, a group said: it means possessors of height, strength and might.

Ibn Fanjawayh informed me, saying: Ibn Hanash related to us, saying: Abu al-Qasim ibn al-Fadl related to us, saying: Abu Hatim related to us, saying: Abu Salih, the scribe of al-Layth, related to us, saying: Muʿawiya ibn Salih related to me from one who related to him, from al-Miqdam, from the Prophet (ﷺ), that he mentioned ﴿Iram of the pillars﴾ and said: "A man among them would come with a rock, carry it on his shoulder, and throw it upon whatever tribe he wished, destroying them."[144][[Tafsir al-Durr al-Manthur: 6/347; Fath al-Bari: 8/538.]]

Al-Kalbi said: the height of a man among them was four hundred cubits. Ibn ʿAbbas said: it means their height was like pillars, and the Arabs call a tall man "muʿammad." Muqatil said: the height of one of them was twelve cubits. Others said: they were only called "of the pillars" because they were people of mobile pillars (tents), who followed the rain and moved to pasture wherever it was, and then returned to their dwellings and did not stay in one place.

Al-Kalbi said: Iram is the one to whom the lineage of ʿAd, Thamud, the people of the Sawad and the people of al-Jazira converge. It used to be said: "ʿAd Iram and Thamud Iram." Then God destroyed ʿAd, then Thamud, and the people of the Sawad and al-Jazira remained. They were people of pillars, tents and livestock in spring, and when the grass withered they returned to their dwellings; they were people of gardens and crops, and their dwellings were in Wadi al-Qura, which is the one of which God says: ﴿the like of which was not created in the lands﴾.

It was also said: they were named "of the pillars" because of a building one of them built, whose pillars he reinforced and whose structure he raised. ʿImad, ʿumud and ʿumud are plurals of ʿamud (pillar).

What Abu al-Qasim the exegete informed us, saying: Abu ʿAbdullah Muhammad ibn ʿAbdullah ibn Ahmad al-Saffar al-Isfahani informed us, saying: Abu Jaʿfar Ahmad ibn Mahdi ibn Rustam al-Isfahani informed us, saying: ʿAbdullah ibn Salih al-Misri related to us, saying: Ibn Lahiʿa related to me. And Abu al-Qasim informed us, saying: Abu al-Hasan Ahmad ibn Muhammad ibn ʿAbdus al-Taraʾifi informed us, saying: ʿUthman ibn Saʿid al-Darji informed us, saying: ʿAbdullah ibn Salih related to us, saying: Ibn Lahiʿa related to me from Khalid ibn Abi ʿImran, from Wahb ibn Munabbih, from ʿAbdullah ibn Qilaba, that he went out seeking camels of his that had strayed. While he was in the deserts of Aden, he came upon a city in those wastelands, with a fortress upon which were great palaces and tall pillars. When he drew near, he thought there was someone there he could ask about his camels, but he saw no one going out or coming in. He dismounted, tethered his mount, drew his sword and entered through the gate of the fortress. When he entered the fortress, he found two enormous gates, larger than any he had seen, both inlaid with white and red rubies. When he saw this he was astonished and amazed, and he opened one of the gates, and there was a city the like of which no one had seen. Each palace had pillars of chrysolite and ruby hanging beneath it, and above each palace were upper chambers:

[Take heed, O you deceived by a long life... I am Shaddad ibn ʿAd, owner of the lofty fortress,
and brother of might and hardship and the gathered kingdom... the abode of the people of the earth fears my threat and warning,
and I ruled East and West with a mighty authority... and by the bounty of kingship, its troops and its multitude,
Then Hud came, and we were in error before Hud... he called us, had we accepted him, to the right course,
but we disobeyed him and cried out, "Is there any escape?" Then a cry came upon us, descending from the distant horizon,
so we were gathered like crops cut down in a wide wilderness.]

﴿And Thamud﴾, that is, and Thamud, ﴿who hewed﴾, meaning carved and cut out, ﴿the rock﴾, the stones, singular "sakhra," ﴿in the valley﴾, meaning the valley of the Qura. They carved houses from them, as God says: ﴿and they used to hew houses out of the mountains, secure﴾.[[Surat al-Hijr: 82.]]

The people of biographical history said: the first to carve mountains, rocks and marble were Thamud. They built from houses and dwellings two thousand and seven hundred thousand, all of stone. Abu Jaʿfar, Abu Hatim and Warsh pronounced the ya' in "al-wad" when pausing and continuing, Ibn Kathir in the narration of al-Bazzi and al-ʿAwwas and Yaʿqub kept it according to the original, while the others omitted it in both situations because it is the end of a verse.

﴿And Pharaoh, possessor of stakes﴾. They differed concerning it. Some said: it means possessor of hosts and armies who strengthened his command and secured his kingdom, and the soldiers were called "stakes" because of the many tents they pitched and fixed on their journeys. This is the narration of ʿAtiyya from Ibn ʿAbbas.

Qatada said: he was called "possessor of stakes" because he had canopies, playgrounds and stakes to which he was tied, and they played beneath them. Muhammad ibn Kaʿb said: it means possessor of firm construction. Saʿid ibn Jubayr said: he had minarets on which he tortured people. Mujahid and others said: he tortured people with stakes; when he became angry with someone he would stretch him on the ground and stake his hands, feet and head to the ground.

Ibn Fanjawayh informed me, saying: Mukhallad related to us, saying: Ibn ʿAlawiyya related to us, saying: Ismaʿil related to us, saying: Ishaq ibn Bishr related to us from Ibn Sam'an, from ʿAta', from Ibn ʿAbbas, that when Pharaoh was told "possessor of stakes," [it was] that she was a woman, namely the woman of his treasurer Kharbil,[[Al-Qurtubi in his tafsir (15/306) cited from al-Tha'labi that his name was Hizqil.]] son of Nuhabil, and he was a believer who concealed his faith for a hundred years,[[As mentioned in Taj al-Arus (7/302); it was also said six hundred years, mentioned by al-Jaza'iri in al-Qisas: 253.]] and he had met some of the companions of Joseph; and his wife was the hairdresser of Pharaoh's daughter. One day, while she was combing the head of Pharaoh's daughter, the comb fell from her hand, and she said: "Woe to the one who disbelieves in God." Pharaoh's daughter said: "Do you have a god other than my father?" She said: "My God and your father's God and the God of the heavens and the earth is one, without partner."

She got up, entered upon her father weeping. He said: "What makes you weep?" She said: "The hairdresser, the woman of your treasurer, claims that your god and her god and the god of the heavens and the earth is one, without partner." He sent for her and asked her about that, and she said: "You have spoken the truth." He said to her: "Woe to you! Disbelieve in your god and affirm that I am your god." She said: "I will not do that." So he stretched her between four stakes, then sent upon her snakes and scorpions, and said to her: "Disbelieve in God, or I will torture you with this torment for two months." She said: "By God, if you tortured me for seventy months I would not disbelieve in God, the Exalted."

He said: She had two daughters, so he brought the elder daughter and slaughtered her in front of her mouth, and said to her: "Disbelieve in God, or I will slaughter your younger daughter in front of your mouth." The younger was a nursing infant, and she felt a great pang for her. She said: "Even if you slaughtered whoever is on the earth in front of my mouth, I would not disbelieve in God, the Exalted."

He said: He brought the daughter, and when she was brought forward, laid down upon her chest and they were about to slaughter her, the mother became distressed. God loosened the tongue of her daughter, and she spoke, for she was one of the four who spoke while infants. She said: "O mother, do not be distressed, for God has built for you a house in Paradise. Be patient, for you are going to the mercy and honor of God." He said: She was slaughtered, and she had not lingered before she died, and God settled her in Paradise.

He said: He sent to seek her husband Kharbil, but they could not find him. It was said to Pharaoh: "He has been seen in such and such a place, in such and such mountains." He sent two men in pursuit of him, and they reached him while he was praying, and three rows of wild beasts were behind him praying. When they saw that, they turned back. Kharbil said: "O God, You know that I concealed my faith for a hundred years, and no one discovered me. Of these two men, whichever concealed [my whereabouts] from me, guide him to Your religion and give him from the world what he asks; and of these two men, whichever revealed me, hasten his punishment in this world, and make his final destination the Fire." The two men returned to Pharaoh. One of them took heed and believed, while the other informed Pharaoh of the story before the chiefs. Pharaoh said to him: "Was there anyone with you other than yourself?" He said: "Yes."

He said: "And who was with you?" He said: "So-and-so." He summoned him. He said: "Is what this one says true?" He said: "No, I did not see anything of what he said." Pharaoh gave him and rewarded him generously. As for the other, he killed him and then crucified him.

He said: Pharaoh had married a woman, one of the most beautiful women of the Children of Israel, called Asiya daughter of Muzahim. When she saw what Pharaoh had done to the hairdresser, she said: "How could I bear to be patient with what Pharaoh has done, while I am a Muslim and he is a disbeliever?" While she was thus deliberating within herself, Pharaoh entered upon her and sat near her. She said: "O Pharaoh, you are the worst and most vile of creatures. You went to the hairdresser and killed her." He said: "Perhaps the madness that afflicted her has also afflicted you."

She said: "I have no madness. My God and your God and the God of the heavens and the earth is one, without partner." He tore at her and beat her, and sent for her parents, summoned them, and told them the matter, that the madness which had afflicted the hairdresser had afflicted her. She said: "I seek refuge in God from that. I testify that my Lord and your Lord and the Lord of the heavens and the earth is one, without partner." Her father said: "O Asiya, are you not the best of the women of the Amalekites, and your husband the god of the Amalekites?" She said: "I seek refuge in God from that, if what you say is true. So tell him: let him crown me with a crown, with the sun in front of it, the moon behind it, and the stars around it." Pharaoh said to them: "Get out of my presence." He stretched her between four stakes to torture her. God opened for her a gate to Paradise to make easier for her what Pharaoh did to her. At that moment she said: ﴿My Lord, build for me near You a house in Paradise, and save me from Pharaoh and his deeds﴾, meaning from Pharaoh's intercourse, ﴿and save me from the wrongdoing people﴾, meaning from Pharaoh and his party. God took her soul and settled her in Paradise.[[The story with variations in the long narrations of al-Tabarani: 115; Tafsir Ibn Kathir: 4/420.]]

It was also said: the stakes are a metaphor for the stability of his kingdom, the length of his reign and the severity of his majesty, like the firmness of stakes in the earth, as the poet al-Aswad said:

﴿In the shade of a king of firm stakes﴾.[[Maʿani al-Qur'an by al-Nahhas: 6/85; Muʿjam al-Buldan: 1/272, whose opening line is: "And they indeed delighted therein in the finest living."]]

﴿Who transgressed in the lands and multiplied corruption therein, so your Lord poured upon them a scourge of punishment.﴾ Qatada said: it means a kind of punishment He poured upon them. Al-Suddi said: every day a different kind of punishment. It was also said: the pain of punishment. The people of the meanings said: this is figurative, because the whip, in their view, is the extreme of punishment, so it applies to every punishment. The poet said:

﴿Do you not see that God has made His religion manifest, and poured upon the disbelievers a whip of punishment?﴾

﴿Indeed your Lord is in the watchtower.﴾ Ibn ʿAbbas said: He, glory be to Him, sees and hears. Muqatil said: He watches over people on the Sirat (bridge), so He placed a watch of angels with them, carrying hooks, staves and thorns. Al-Dahhak said: in a watchtower over the people of wrongdoing and disobedience. It was also said: its meaning is that the return of creation and their destination is to His judgment and command. Al-Hasan and ʿIkrima said: He watches the deeds of the children of Adam. Also from Muqatil: their passing by it. ʿAta' ibn Abi Rabah: no one escapes Him. Yaman: there is no escape from Him. Al-Suddi: He sets the Fire on their paths until it destroys them. The word "al-mirsad" and "al-marsad" mean the path, and the plural of "al-mirsad" is "marasid," and the plural of "al-marsad" is "marasid."

Muqsim narrated from Ibn ʿAbbas, who said: Over Hell there are seven checkpoints. The servants are questioned at the first of them about the testimony that there is no god but God. If he brings it complete, he passes to the second, where he is asked about prayer. If he brings it complete, he passes to the third, where he is asked about zakat. If he brings it complete, he passes to the fourth, where he is asked about fasting. If he brings it complete, he passes to the fifth, where he is asked about Hajj. If he brings it complete, he passes to the sixth, where he is asked about 'Umra. If he brings it complete, he passes to the seventh, where he is asked about wrongful acts. If he is clear of them, well; otherwise it is said, "Wait and see." If he has voluntary acts, they complete his deeds, and when he has finished with them he is taken to Paradise.

She said: "I will not do that." So he stretched her between four stakes, then sent upon her snakes and scorpions, and said to her: "Disbelieve in God, or I will torture you with this torment for two months." She said: "By God, if you tortured me for seventy months I would not disbelieve in God, the Exalted."

He said: She had two daughters, so he brought the elder daughter and slaughtered her in front of her mouth, and said to her: "Disbelieve in God, or I will slaughter your younger daughter in front of your mouth." The younger was a nursing infant, and she felt a great pang for her. She said: "Even if you slaughtered whoever is on the earth in front of my mouth, I would not disbelieve in God, the Exalted."

He said: He brought the daughter, and when she was brought forward, laid down upon her chest and they were about to slaughter her, the mother became distressed. God loosened the tongue of her daughter, and she spoke, for she was one of the four who spoke while infants. She said: "O mother, do not be distressed, for God has built for you a house in Paradise. Be patient, for you are going to the mercy and honor of God." He said: She was slaughtered, and she had not lingered before she died, and God settled her in Paradise.

He said: He sent to seek her husband Kharbil, but they could not find him. It was said to Pharaoh: "He has been seen in such and such a place, in such and such mountains." He sent two men in pursuit of him, and they reached him while he was praying, and three rows of wild beasts were behind him praying. When they saw that, they turned back. Kharbil said: "O God, You know that I concealed my faith for a hundred years, and no one discovered me. Of these two men, whichever concealed [my whereabouts] from me, guide him to Your religion and give him from the world what he asks; and of these two men, whichever revealed me, hasten his punishment in this world, and make his final destination the Fire." The two men returned to Pharaoh. One of them took heed and believed, while the other informed Pharaoh of the story before the chiefs. Pharaoh said to him: "Was there anyone with you other than yourself?" He said: "Yes."

He said: "And who was with you?" He said: "So-and-so." He summoned him. He said: "Is what this one says true?" He said: "No, I did not see anything of what he said." Pharaoh gave him and rewarded him generously. As for the other, he killed him and then crucified him.

He said: Pharaoh had married a woman, one of the most beautiful women of the Children of Israel, called Asiya daughter of Muzahim. When she saw what Pharaoh had done to the hairdresser, she said: "How could I bear to be patient with what Pharaoh has done, while I am a Muslim and he is a disbeliever?" While she was thus deliberating within herself, Pharaoh entered upon her and sat near her. She said: "O Pharaoh, you are the worst and most vile of creatures. You went to the hairdresser and killed her." He said: "Perhaps the madness that afflicted her has also afflicted you."

She said: "I have no madness. My God and your God and the God of the heavens and the earth is one, without partner." He tore at her and beat her, and sent for her parents, summoned them, and told them the matter, that the madness which had afflicted the hairdresser had afflicted her. She said: "I seek refuge in God from that. I testify that my Lord and your Lord and the Lord of the heavens and the earth is one, without partner." Her father said: "O Asiya, are you not the best of the women of the Amalekites, and your husband the god of the Amalekites?" She said: "I seek refuge in God from that, if what you say is true. Muhammad ibn Kaʿb said: it means possessor of firm construction. Saʿid ibn Jubayr said: he had minarets on which he tortured people. Mujahid and others said: he tortured people with stakes; when he became angry with someone he would stretch him on the ground and stake his hands, feet and head to the ground.

Ibn Fanjawayh informed me, saying: Mukhallad related to us, saying: Ibn ʿAlawiyya related to us, saying: Ismaʿil related to us, saying: Ishaq ibn Bishr related to us from Ibn Sam'an, from ʿAta', from Ibn ʿAbbas, that when Pharaoh was told "possessor of stakes," [it was] that she was a woman, namely the woman of his treasurer Kharbil,[[Al-Qurtubi in his tafsir (15/306) cited from al-Tha'labi that his name was Hizqil.]] son of Nuhabil, and he was a believer who concealed his faith for a hundred years,[[As mentioned in Taj al-Arus (7/302); it was also said six hundred years, mentioned by al-Jaza'iri in al-Qisas: 253.]] and he had met some of the companions of Joseph; and his wife was the hairdresser of Pharaoh's daughter. One day, while she was combing the head of Pharaoh's daughter, the comb fell from her hand, and she said: "Woe to the one who disbelieves in God." Pharaoh's daughter said: "Do you have a god other than my father?" She said: "My God and your father's God and the God of the heavens and the earth is one, without partner."

She got up, entered upon her father weeping. He said: "What makes you weep?" She said: "The hairdresser, the woman of your treasurer, claims that your god and her god and the god of the heavens and the earth is one, without partner." He sent for her and asked her about that, and she said: "You have spoken the truth." He said to her: "Woe to you! Disbelieve in your god and affirm that I am your god." She said: "I will not do that." So he stretched her between four stakes, then sent upon her snakes and scorpions, and said to her: "Disbelieve in God, or I will torture you with this torment for two months." She said: "By God, if you tortured me for seventy months I would not disbelieve in God, the Exalted."

He said: She had two daughters, so he brought the elder daughter and slaughtered her in front of her mouth, and said to her: "Disbelieve in God, or I will slaughter your younger daughter in front of your mouth." The younger was a nursing infant, and she felt a great pang for her. She said: "Even if you slaughtered whoever is on the earth in front of my mouth, I would not disbelieve in God, the Exalted."

He said: He brought the daughter, and when she was brought forward, laid down upon her chest and they were about to slaughter her, the mother became distressed. God loosened the tongue of her daughter, and she spoke, for she was one of the four who spoke while infants. She said: "O mother, do not be distressed, for God has built for you a house in Paradise. Be patient, for you are going to the mercy and honor of God." He said: She was slaughtered, and she had not lingered before she died, and God settled her in Paradise.

He said: He sent to seek her husband Kharbil, but they could not find him. It was said to Pharaoh: "He has been seen in such and such a place, in such and such mountains." He sent two men in pursuit of him, and they reached him while he was praying, and three rows of wild beasts were behind him praying. When they saw that, they turned back. Kharbil said: "O God, You know that I concealed my faith for a hundred years, and no one discovered me. Of these two men, whichever concealed [my whereabouts] from me, guide him to Your religion and give him from the world what he asks; and of these two men, whichever revealed me, hasten his punishment in this world, and make his final destination the Fire." The two men returned to Pharaoh. One of them took heed and believed, while the other informed Pharaoh of the story before the chiefs. Pharaoh said to him: "Was there anyone with you other than yourself?" He said: "Yes."

He said: "And who was with you?" He said: "So-and-so." He summoned him. He said: "Is what this one says true?" He said: "No, I did not see anything of what he said." Pharaoh gave him and rewarded him generously. As for the other, he killed him and then crucified him.

He said: Pharaoh had married a woman, one of the most beautiful women of the Children of Israel, called Asiya daughter of Muzahim. When she saw what Pharaoh had done to the hairdresser, she said: "How could I bear to be patient with what Pharaoh has done, while I am a Muslim and he is a disbeliever?" While she was thus deliberating within herself, Pharaoh entered upon her and sat near her. She said: "O Pharaoh, you are the worst and most vile of creatures. You went to the hairdresser and killed her." He said: "Perhaps the madness that afflicted her has also afflicted you."

She said: "I have no madness. My God and your God and the God of the heavens and the earth is one, without partner." He tore at her and beat her, and sent for her parents, summoned them, and told them the matter, that the madness which had afflicted the hairdresser had afflicted her. She said: "I seek refuge in God from that. I testify that my Lord and your Lord and the Lord of the heavens and the earth is one, without partner." Her father said: "O Asiya, are you not the best of the women of the Amalekites, and your husband the god of the Amalekites?" She said: "I seek refuge in God from that, if what you say is true. So tell him: let him crown me with a crown, with the sun in front of it, the moon behind it, and the stars around it." Pharaoh said to them: "Get out of my presence." He stretched her between four stakes to torture her. God opened for her a gate to Paradise to make easier for her what Pharaoh did to her. At that moment she said: ﴿My Lord, build for me near You a house in Paradise, and save me from Pharaoh and his deeds﴾, meaning from Pharaoh's intercourse, ﴿and save me from the wrongdoing people﴾, meaning from Pharaoh and his party. God took her soul and settled her in Paradise.[[The story with variations in the long narrations of al-Tabarani: 115; Tafsir Ibn Kathir: 4/420.]]

It was also said: the stakes are a metaphor for the stability of his kingdom, the length of his reign and the severity of his majesty, like the firmness of stakes in the earth, as the poet al-Aswad said:

﴿In the shade of a king of firm stakes﴾.[[Maʿani al-Qur'an by al-Nahhas: 6/85; Muʿjam al-Buldan: 1/272, whose opening line is: "And they indeed delighted therein in the finest living."]]

﴿Who transgressed in the lands and multiplied corruption therein, so your Lord poured upon them a scourge of punishment.﴾ Qatada said: it means a kind of punishment He poured upon them. Al-Suddi said: every day a different kind of punishment. It was also said: the pain of punishment. The people of the meanings said: this is figurative, because the whip, in their view, is the extreme of punishment, so it applies to every punishment. The poet said:

﴿Do you not see that God has made His religion manifest, and poured upon the disbelievers a whip of punishment?﴾

﴿Indeed your Lord is in the watchtower.﴾ Ibn ʿAbbas said: He, glory be to Him, sees and hears. Muqatil said: He watches over people on the Sirat (bridge), so He placed a watch of angels with them, carrying hooks, staves and thorns. Al-Dahhak said: in a watchtower over the people of wrongdoing and disobedience. It was also said: its meaning is that the return of creation and their destination is to His judgment and command. Al-Hasan and ʿIkrima said: He watches the deeds of the children of Adam. Also from Muqatil: their passing by it. ʿAta' ibn Abi Rabah: no one escapes Him. Yaman: there is no escape from Him. Al-Suddi: He sets the Fire on their paths until it destroys them. The word "al-mirsad" and "al-marsad" mean the path, and the plural of "al-mirsad" is "marasid," and the plural of "al-marsad" is "marasid."

Muqsim narrated from Ibn ʿAbbas, who said: Over Hell there are seven checkpoints. The servants are questioned at the first of them about the testimony that there is no god but God. If he brings it complete, he passes to the second, where he is asked about prayer. If he brings it complete, he passes to the third, where he is asked about zakat. If he brings it complete, he passes to the fourth, where he is asked about fasting. If he brings it complete, he passes to the fifth, where he is asked about Hajj. If he brings it complete, he passes to the sixth, where he is asked about 'Umra. If he brings it complete, he passes to the seventh, where he is asked about wrongful acts. If he is clear of them, well; otherwise it is said, "Wait and see." If he has voluntary acts, they complete his deeds, and when he has finished with them he is taken to Paradise.

Commentary of al-Tha'alibi (al-Jawahir al-Hisan) on Surah 89, verses 6–14:

﴿Have you not seen how your Lord dealt with 'Ad, Iram,﴾. The common readers recited it with tanwin (ʿĀdin, Iraman). Al-Hasan recited (bi-ʿĀdi Iram) as an idafa (construct). The common readers recited (Iram) with a kasra on the alif, while Mujahid recited it with a fatha. The historian said: whoever recites it with a fatha on the alif likens them to the ārām (landmarks), whose singular is ārim.

The scholars differed over the meaning of His words ﴿Iram﴾. Ibn Fanjawayh informed me, saying: Musa al-Baqirhi related to us, saying: Ibn ʿAlawiyya related to us, saying: Ismaʿil related to us, saying: Ishaq ibn Bishr related to us from Muhammad ibn Ishaq, from someone who told him that Saʿid ibn al-Musayyab used to say: ﴿Iram of the pillars, Damascus﴾.

Ibn Fanjawayh also informed me, saying: Ibn Hamdan related to us, saying: Ibn Marwan related to us, saying: ʿAli ibn Harb al-Tai related to us, saying: Abu al-Ashhab Hud related to us from ʿAwf al-Aʿrabi, from Khalid al-Rabʿi, regarding ﴿Iram of the pillars﴾, that he said: Damascus. Ikrima and Abu Saʿid al-Maqburi also said this.

Al-Qurazi said: it is Alexandria. Mujahid said: it is Irama, meaning "the ancient." Qatada said: they are a tribe of ʿAd. Abu Ishaq said: it is the grandfather of ʿAd, namely ʿAd ibn ʿAwis ibn Iram ibn Sam ibn Nuh.

Muqatil said: Iram is a tribe from the people of ʿAd in which kingship resided, and they were the place of Mahra. ʿAd was their father, so they were attributed to him. He is Iram ibn ʿAd ibn Shamr ibn Sam ibn Nuh.

Ibn Fanjawayh informed us, saying: Ibn Hanash related to us, saying: Abu al-Tayyib al-Marwazi related to us, saying: Muhammad ibn ʿAli related to us, saying: Fadl ibn Khalid informed us, saying: ʿUbayd ibn Sulayman related to us from al-Dahhak ibn Muzahim that he used to recite ﴿Iram of the pillars﴾ with a fatha on the alif and the ra', and that Iram means destruction. He said: "Arama banu fulan," meaning they were destroyed. This is also the narration of al-ʿAwfi from Ibn ʿAbbas.

It is also narrated from al-Dahhak that he recited ﴿Iram of the pillars﴾, meaning: He destroyed them and made them crumbled bones (rumim). The correct view is that it is the name of a tribe or a town, and therefore it is not inflected (with kasra).[[Tafsir al-Tabari: 30/220.]]

As for His words ﴿of the pillars﴾, a group said: it means possessors of height, strength and might.

Ibn Fanjawayh informed me, saying: Ibn Hanash related to us, saying: Abu al-Qasim ibn al-Fadl related to us, saying: Abu Hatim related to us, saying: Abu Salih, the scribe of al-Layth, related to us, saying: Muʿawiya ibn Salih related to me from one who related to him, from al-Miqdam, from the Prophet (ﷺ), that he mentioned ﴿Iram of the pillars﴾ and said: "A man among them would come with a rock, carry it on his shoulder, and throw it upon whatever tribe he wished, destroying them."[144][[Tafsir al-Durr al-Manthur: 6/347; Fath al-Bari: 8/538.]]

Al-Kalbi said: the height of a man among them was four hundred cubits. Ibn ʿAbbas said: it means their height was like pillars, and the Arabs call a tall man "muʿammad." Muqatil said: the height of one of them was twelve cubits. Others said: they were only called "of the pillars" because they were people of mobile pillars (tents), who followed the rain and moved to pasture wherever it was, and then returned to their dwellings and did not stay in one place.

Al-Kalbi said: Iram is the one to whom the lineage of ʿAd, Thamud, the people of the Sawad and the people of al-Jazira converge. It used to be said: "ʿAd Iram and Thamud Iram." Then God destroyed ʿAd, then Thamud, and the people of the Sawad and al-Jazira remained. They were people of pillars, tents and livestock in spring, and when the grass withered they returned to their dwellings; they were people of gardens and crops, and their dwellings were in Wadi al-Qura, which is the one of which God says: ﴿the like of which was not created in the lands﴾.

It was also said: they were named "of the pillars" because of a building one of them built, whose pillars he reinforced and whose structure he raised. ʿImad, ʿumud and ʿumud are plurals of ʿamud (pillar).

What Abu al-Qasim the exegete informed us, saying: Abu ʿAbdullah Muhammad ibn ʿAbdullah ibn Ahmad al-Saffar al-Isfahani informed us, saying: Abu Jaʿfar Ahmad ibn Mahdi ibn Rustam al-Isfahani informed us, saying: ʿAbdullah ibn Salih al-Misri related to us, saying: Ibn Lahiʿa related to me. And Abu al-Qasim informed us, saying: Abu al-Hasan Ahmad ibn Muhammad ibn ʿAbdus al-Taraʾifi informed us, saying: ʿUthman ibn Saʿid al-Darji informed us, saying: ʿAbdullah ibn Salih related to us, saying: Ibn Lahiʿa related to me from Khalid ibn Abi ʿImran, from Wahb ibn Munabbih, from ʿAbdullah ibn Qilaba, that he went out seeking camels of his that had strayed. While he was in the deserts of Aden, he came upon a city in those wastelands, with a fortress upon which were great palaces and tall pillars. When he drew near, he thought there was someone there he could ask about his camels, but he saw no one going out or coming in. He dismounted, tethered his mount, drew his sword and entered through the gate of the fortress. When he entered the fortress, he found two enormous gates, larger than any he had seen, both inlaid with white and red rubies. When he saw this he was astonished and amazed, and he opened one of the gates, and there was a city the like of which no one had seen. Each palace had pillars of chrysolite and ruby hanging beneath it, and above each palace were upper chambers:

[Take heed, O you deceived by a long life... I am Shaddad ibn ʿAd, owner of the lofty fortress,
and brother of might and hardship and the gathered kingdom... the abode of the people of the earth fears my threat and warning,
and I ruled East and West with a mighty authority... and by the bounty of kingship, its troops and its multitude,
Then Hud came, and we were in error before Hud... he called us, had we accepted him, to the right course,
but we disobeyed him and cried out, "Is there any escape?" Then a cry came upon us, descending from the distant horizon,
so we were gathered like crops cut down in a wide wilderness.]

﴿And Thamud﴾, that is, and Thamud, ﴿who hewed﴾, meaning carved and cut out, ﴿the rock﴾, the stones, singular "sakhra," ﴿in the valley﴾, meaning the valley of the Qura. They carved houses from them, as God says: ﴿and they used to hew houses out of the mountains, secure﴾.[[Surat al-Hijr: 82.]]

The people of biographical history said: the first to carve mountains, rocks and marble were Thamud. They built from houses and dwellings two thousand and seven hundred thousand, all of stone. Abu Jaʿfar, Abu Hatim and Warsh pronounced the ya' in "al-wad" when pausing and continuing, Ibn Kathir in the narration of al-Bazzi and al-ʿAwwas and Yaʿqub kept it according to the original, while the others omitted it in both situations because it is the end of a verse.

Some said: it means possessor of hosts and armies who strengthened his command and secured his kingdom, and the soldiers were called "stakes" because of the many tents they pitched and fixed on their journeys. One day, while she was combing the head of Pharaoh's daughter, the comb fell from her hand, and she said: "Woe to the one who disbelieves in God." Pharaoh's daughter said: "Do you have a god other than my father?" She said: "My God and your father's God and the God of the heavens and the earth is one, without partner."

She said: "By God, if you tortured me for seventy months I would not disbelieve in God, the Exalted."

He said: She had two daughters, so he brought the elder daughter and slaughtered her in front of her mouth, and said to her: "Disbelieve in God, or I will slaughter your younger daughter in front of your mouth." **Commentary of al-Tha'labi (al-Jawahir al-Hisan) on Surah 89, verses 15–30**

﴿As for man, when his Lord tests him by giving him honor and abundance﴾: that is, He tries him with blessing and plenty. ﴿He honors him with wealth and bestows on him favors through what He has widened for him, so he says: "My Lord has honored me,"﴾ and so he rejoices, is glad, praises Him for it and gives thanks. ﴿But when He tests him by restricting his provision, measuring it out and straitening his sustenance, he says: "My Lord has humiliated me,"﴾ that is, has disgraced me with poverty. He does not thank Allah for what He has given him of soundness of limbs and the health and well-being He has provided. Qatadah said: "How quickly the son of Adam becomes ungrateful!"

The recitation of the majority is ﴿fa-qadara﴾ with a light *dal*. Abu Ja'far and Ibn 'Amir read it with a doubled *dal* (*faqqadara*). Both are dialectal variants. Abu 'Amr used to say: *qadara* means *qattara* (to restrict), and *qaddara* means to give him what suffices him. Had it been the latter, he would not have said, "My Lord has humiliated me." Then He responded to him, saying: ﴿No!﴾ I did not test him with wealth because of his honor with Me, nor did I test him with poverty because of his lowliness with Me. Poverty and wealth are part of My decree and My judgment. So I do not honor the one to whom I have given wealth and abundance of the world, nor do I humiliate the one whom I have humbled with poverty and scarcity of the world. Rather, I honor the one who honors Me by obedience, and I humiliate the one who humbles himself by disobedience to Me. Al-Farra' said: the meaning of *kalla* (no) is that it is not fitting for him to be this way; rather, it is fitting that he praise Him for both circumstances, wealth and poverty.

Then He said: ﴿Nay, but you do not honor the orphan﴾, meaning: I humiliated the one I humiliated because he does not honor the orphan.

The reciters differed regarding this verse. The people of Basra read *yukrimūna* and what follows it entirely with the *yā'* (third person), while the others read it with the *tā'* (second person). ﴿And you do not urge one another to feed the needy﴾: Abu Ja'far and the people of Kufa read *tahāḍḍūna* with an *alif* and an open *tā'*. Al-Shadhhari related from al-Kisa'i *tuḥāḍḍūna* with a *ḍammah* on the *tā'*. Others read *taḥuḍḍūna* without the *alif*. ﴿And you devour the inheritance greedily﴾: *al-turāth* is the inheritance, and *aklan lamman* means intense, excessive eating. Al-Hasan said: he eats his own share and the share of others. Bakr ibn 'Abd Allah said: *al-lamm* is transgression in inheritance; he consumes his own inheritance and that of others. Ibn Zayd said: *al-akl al-lamm* is the eating of one who devours everything he finds without asking whether it is lawful or unlawful, consuming what is his and what belongs to others. This was because they did not give inheritance to women or children. [The verse] ﴿They ask you concerning women. Say: Allah gives you a ruling concerning them﴾ and so on was recited. Abu 'Ubayda said: it is said, *lammtu mā 'alā al-khiwān* (I licked up what was on the tray), when one reaches what is on it and eats it all together.

﴿And you love wealth with an abundant love﴾: *jamman* means much, abundant. It is said *jamma al-mā' fī al-ḥawḍ* (the water gathered in the basin) when it became abundant and collected. ﴿No!﴾ This is not how the matter ought to be. Then He informed about those who lament over what they have passed by, when it will no longer benefit them, saying, exalted is He who speaks:

﴿When the earth is pounded to powder, powder upon powder﴾: meaning, repeatedly, time after time, so that everything upon it is crushed.

﴿And your Lord comes﴾: al-Hasan said: His command and His judgment. The people of spiritual allusion (*ahl al-ishārah*) said: the manifestation of your Lord's power. Matters are settled, and the Truth cannot be described as moving from place to place; how could He move about or travel, when He has no place or time, and no moment or duration applies to Him? For to be deprived of a moment regarding something means to miss the moments, and whoever misses something is incapable, whereas the Truth is far above having His attributes contained by natures or encompassed by hearts.

﴿And the angels come in ranks, rank upon rank, and on that Day Hell is brought near﴾.

Ibn Fanjawayh informed me, saying: Ibn Majah told us, saying: Ya'qub ibn Yusuf al-Qarawi told us, saying: al-Qasim ibn al-Hakam told us, saying: 'Ubayd Allah ibn al-Walid told us, saying: 'Atiyyah told us, from Abu Sa'id, who said: When this verse was revealed, ﴿And on that Day Hell is brought near﴾, the color of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) changed and sweat appeared on his face, to the extent that what his companions saw of his condition weighed heavily upon them. Some of them went to 'Ali (may Allah be pleased with him) and said: "O 'Ali, something has happened which we have seen in the Prophet of Allah (ﷺ)." So 'Ali came, embraced him from behind, kissed between his shoulders, and said: "O Prophet of Allah, may my father and mother be your ransom, what has happened today and what has changed you?"

He said: "Jibril (peace be upon him) came and recited to me this verse: ﴿No! When the earth is pounded to powder, powder upon powder, and your Lord comes, and the angels in ranks, rank upon rank, and on that Day Hell is brought near.﴾" I said: "How will it be brought?" He said: "Seventy thousand angels will bring it, leading it by seventy thousand bridles, and it will break loose with such a plunge that if it were left it would burn the people of the gathering. Then Hell will confront me and say: 'What is between me and you, O Muhammad? Allah has forbidden your flesh and blood to me.' No one will remain except that he says: 'myself, myself,' while Muhammad says: 'my nation, my nation.' Then Allah, glory be to Him, will say to the angels: 'Do you not see the people saying: "My Lord, myself, myself," while Muhammad says: "my nation, my nation"?'"[145] [[Tafsir al-Qurtubi: 20/56.]]

Abdullah ibn Mas'ud and Muqatil said regarding this verse: Hell will be led by seventy thousand *zamān* (chains or bridles), each bridle in the hand of seventy thousand angels; it will roar and groan until it is placed on the left of the Throne.

﴿On that Day man will remember, but how will the reminder benefit him?﴾ ﴿He will say: "Would that I had sent ahead for my life"﴾, that is, for my life in the Hereafter. ﴿On that Day none will punish as He punishes, and none will bind as He binds.﴾ The majority read it with a *kasrah* on the *dhāl* and the *thā'* (*yu'adhdhibu* and *yūthiqu*), meaning: no one in this world punishes like Allah's punishment on that Day.

Al-Farra' said: it was also said that this refers to a specific man, Umayyah ibn Khalaf al-Jumahi. The meaning is: no one punishes like the punishment of this disbeliever, and no one binds like his binding. Abu 'Ubayd and Abu Hatim preferred this recitation, because:

Muhammad ibn Nu'aym informed us, saying: al-Husayn ibn Ayyub informed us, saying: 'Ali ibn 'Abd al-'Aziz informed us, saying: al-Qasim ibn Sallam informed us, saying: Hushaym and 'Abbad ibn 'Abbad told us, from Khalid al-Hadhdha', from Abu Qilabah, from one whom the Prophet (ﷺ) had taught to recite, *fa-yawma'idhin lā yu'adhdhabu 'adhābahu aḥadun wa lā yūthaqu wathāqahu aḥad*, with the *dhāl* and *thā'* pronounced with a *fatḥah*.

It is also related that Abu 'Amr returned in the last part of his life to the recitation of the Prophet (ﷺ).

The meaning of the verse is: no one among creation reaches the extent of Allah's punishment and binding, and that is the reference to the chains and the shackles.

Ibn Fanjawayh informed us, saying: Ibn Malik told us, saying: Ibn Hanbal told us, saying: my father told me, saying:

Muhammad ibn Ja'far told us, saying: Shu'bah told us, from Khalid al-Hadhdha', from Abu Qilabah, from one who heard the Prophet (ﷺ) recite *fa-yawma'idhin lā yu'adhdhibu 'adhābahu aḥadun wa lā yūthiqu wathāqahu aḥad*, meaning: "no one does to him."

﴿O soul at rest﴾, content with what Allah has promised, confirming what He has said.

Mujahid said: *al-munība* is the humble and submissive one who has become certain that Allah, glory be to Him, is our Lord, and who has steeled her heart for His command.

Al-Musayyib said: I heard al-Kalbi and Abu Rawq say: it is the one whose face Allah whitens, and to whom He gives her book in her right hand; then at that moment she is at rest. Al-Hasan said: the believing and certain one. 'Atiyyah said: the one content with Allah's decree. Hayyan, from al-Kalbi: the one safe from the punishment of Allah, exalted is He.[[Tafsir al-Tabari: 30/238.]]

'Aqil informed me that Abu al-Faraj informed them, from Ibn Jarir, who said: Khallad ibn Aslam told us, saying: al-Nadr informed us, from Harun al-Qari', who said: Hilal told me, from Abu Shaykh al-Hana'i, who said: in the recitation of Ubayy: *yā ayyatuhā al-nafs al-āminatu al-muṭma'innah* (O soul, secure and at rest).

Abu Muhammad al-Husayn ibn Ahmad al-Sha'bi informed me, saying: my father told me, saying: Muhammad ibn Ishaq al-Siraj told us, saying: Sawwar ibn 'Abd Allah told us, saying: al-Mu'ammar ibn Sulayman told us, from Ibrahim ibn Isma'il, from Ibn Abi Najih, from Mujahid, regarding *yā ayyatuhā al-nafs al-muṭma'innah*: he said: the one content with Allah's decree, who knows that what befell her would not have missed her, and that what missed her would not have befallen her. Ibn Kaysan said: the sincere one. Ibn 'Ata': she is the one who knows Allah, glory be to Him, and does not turn away from Him for the blink of an eye. It was also said: the one at rest through the remembrance of Allah. Its explanation is: ﴿and their hearts find rest in the remembrance of Allah﴾. It was also said: she is the one who trusts in Allah, exalted is He, and is confident in what He has guaranteed her of provision.[[See Tafsir al-Qurtubi: 20/57.]]

﴿Return to your Lord﴾. The scholars differed in interpreting this verse and the time of this saying. Some people said: it is said to her at death: ﴿Return to your Lord﴾, who is Allah, mighty and majestic.

Al-Husayn informed me, saying: 'Ubayd Allah ibn 'Abd Allah ibn Abi Samurah al-Baghawi told us, saying: Muhammad ibn Sahl al-'Askari told us, saying: al-'Ataridi told us, saying: my father told us, saying: Qays ibn al-Rabi' told us, from Isma'il, from Abu Salih, regarding His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Return to your Lord, content and pleasing﴾: he said: this is at her departure from the world, and when the Day of Resurrection comes, it will be said: ﴿Enter among My servants, and enter My Paradise.﴾

Ibn Fanjawayh informed me, saying: Ibn Shanbah told us, saying: al-Furati told us, saying: Ahmad ibn Khalid told us, saying: Rawh ibn 'Ubadah told us, saying: Zuhayr ibn Muhammad told us, saying: Zayd ibn Aslam told us, from 'Abd al-Rahman ibn al-Sulaymani, from 'Abd Allah ibn 'Amr ibn al-'As, who said: When the believing servant dies, Allah, glory be to Him, sends two angels, and sends to him a gift from Paradise. It is said to her: "Come out, O soul at rest, come out to rest and fragrance, and a Lord who is well pleased with you." She comes out like the finest scent of musk that anyone ever smelled, and the angels are on the edges of the heaven.

They say: "A good spirit has come from the earth, a good breath." No gate is passed except that it is opened for her, and no angel except that he prays for her, until she is brought before the Merciful. Then the angels prostrate, and they say: "Our Lord, this is Your servant so-and-so, who used to worship You and never associated anything with You." He says: "Tell him to prostrate," and the soul prostrates. Then Mikail is called, and He says: "Take her and place her with the souls of the believers until I ask you about her on the Day of Resurrection." Then he is commanded, and his grave is widened for him seventy cubits in width and seventy cubits in length, and fragrant plants grow for him in it. If he had any Qur'an with him, its light suffices him; if he did not, a likeness of the sun is made for him in his grave, and he is like a bride who sleeps, and no one wakes her except the dearest of her family to her, so she rises from her sleep as if she had not had enough of it. When the disbeliever dies, Allah, glory be to Him and exalted, sends two angels and sends with them a piece of the most foul and rough cloth of every rough thing, and it is said: "O wicked soul, come out to scalding water and painful punishment, and your Lord is angry with you."

Ibn Fanjawayh informed me, saying: Ibn Hamdan told us, saying: al-Masuhi told us, saying: 'Amr ibn al-'Ala' al-Hanafi told us, saying: Ibn Yaman told us, from Ash'ath, from Ja'far, from Sa'id, who said: A man recited before the Prophet (ﷺ), *yā ayyatuhā al-nafs al-muṭma'innah*. Abu Bakr said: "How beautiful this is!" The Prophet (ﷺ) said: "Indeed, the angel will say it to you [at death]."[[Kanz al-'Ummal: 12/485, no. 35591; what is between brackets is from it.]]

Ahmad ibn Muhammad ibn Ya'qub al-Qasri informed us there, saying: Isma'il ibn Muhammad ibn Isma'il informed us in Baghdad, saying: al-Hasan ibn 'Arafah told us, saying: Marwan ibn Shuja' al-Jazari informed me. And Ibn Fanjawayh informed me, saying: Ibn Shanbah told us, saying: Muhammad ibn 'Ali ibn Salim told us, saying: Ahmad ibn Munay' told us, saying: Marwan told us, from Salim al-Aftas, from Sa'id ibn Jubayr, who said: Ibn 'Abbas died at al-Ta'if, and a bird came, which was not seen in its form, and entered his bier, and then it was not seen leaving it. When he was buried, this verse was recited at the edge of the grave, and the one reciting it was not seen: ﴿O soul at rest, return to your Lord, content and pleasing, so enter among My servants and enter My Paradise.﴾

Others said: it is only said to her at the Resurrection: ﴿Return to your Lord﴾, that is, to your companion, your body. So Allah, glory be to Him, commands the spirits to return to the bodies. This view was held by 'Ikrimah, 'Ata', al-Dahhak, and it is the narration of al-'Awfi from Ibn 'Abbas.

The evidence for this interpretation is what Muhammad ibn Nu'aym informed us, saying: al-Husayn ibn Ayyub informed us, saying: 'Ali ibn 'Abd al-'Aziz informed us, saying: al-Qasim ibn Sallam told us, saying: Hajjaj told us, from Harun, from Aban ibn Abi 'Ayyash, from Sulayman ibn Qitah, from Ibn 'Abbas, that he recited it as *fa-dkhulī fī 'abdī* ("enter among My servant"), with the monotheistic reading.

Al-Hasan said: its meaning is: return to the reward of your Lord and His honor. Ibn Kaysan said: ﴿Return to your Lord﴾, that is, those like you among the righteous servants of your Lord.

Some people of spiritual allusion said: ﴿O soul at rest﴾ in the world, ﴿return to Allah﴾ by leaving it; and returning to Allah is following the path of the Hereafter. ﴿Content﴾ with Allah in what He has prepared for her, ﴿pleasing﴾ to her Lord, who is pleased with her. ﴿So enter among My servants﴾. Some said: that is, with My servants, ﴿My Paradise﴾; the meaning of the verse involves inversion and reordering, and this was the view of Muqatil, al-Qurazi and Abu 'Ubaydah. ﴿And enter, by Your mercy, among Your righteous servants﴾, that is, with Our prophets in Paradise. Al-Akhfash said: that is, among My party. And another said: it is the command for the spirits to return to their bodies. And Allah knows best.

Ibn Fanjawayh informed me, saying: Musa ibn Muhammad told us, saying: Ibn 'Alawiyyah told us, saying: Isma'il told us, saying: al-Musayyib told us, saying: Ibrahim told us, from Salih ibn Hayyan, from Ibn Buraydah, regarding this verse, ﴿O soul at rest﴾, he said: it is the soul of Hamzah ibn 'Abd al-Muttalib; it was revealed concerning him on the day he was martyred at Uhud. Rather, his soul descended in the presence of the Lord of the worlds, honored and exalted above those near Him, until Allah, glory be to Him, returns it to Hamzah in tranquility, calm, and honor.

It was also revealed concerning Habib ibn 'Adi, whom the people of Makkah crucified and turned his face toward Madinah. He said: "O Allah, if I have any good with You, turn my face toward Your qibla." So Allah, glory be to Him, turned his face toward the qibla without anyone turning it, and no one could turn it. Its ruling is general for all believers who are at rest.

**Commentary of al-Tha'labi (al-Jawahir al-Hisan) on Surah 89, verses 15–30**

﴿As for man, when his Lord tests him by giving him honor and abundance﴾: that is, He tries him with blessing and plenty. ﴿He honors him with wealth and bestows on him favors through what He has widened for him, so he says: "My Lord has honored me,"﴾ and so he rejoices, is glad, praises Him for it and gives thanks. ﴿But when He tests him by restricting his provision, measuring it out and straitening his sustenance, he says: "My Lord has humiliated me,"﴾ that is, has disgraced me with poverty. He does not thank Allah for what He has given him of soundness of limbs and the health and well-being He has provided. Qatadah said: "How quickly the son of Adam becomes ungrateful!"

The recitation of the majority is ﴿fa-qadara﴾ with a light *dal*. Abu Ja'far and Ibn 'Amir read it with a doubled *dal* (*faqqadara*). Both are dialectal variants. Abu 'Amr used to say: *qadara* means *qattara* (to restrict), and *qaddara* means to give him what suffices him. Had it been the latter, he would not have said, "My Lord has humiliated me." Then He responded to him, saying: ﴿No!﴾ I did not test him with wealth because of his honor with Me, nor did I test him with poverty because of his lowliness with Me. Poverty and wealth are part of My decree and My judgment. So I do not honor the one to whom I have given wealth and abundance of the world, nor do I humiliate the one whom I have humbled with poverty and scarcity of the world. Rather, I honor the one who honors Me by obedience, and I humiliate the one who humbles himself by disobedience to Me. Al-Farra' said: the meaning of *kalla* (no) is that it is not fitting for him to be this way; rather, it is fitting that he praise Him for both circumstances, wealth and poverty.

Then He said: ﴿Nay, but you do not honor the orphan﴾, meaning: I humiliated the one I humiliated because he does not honor the orphan.

The reciters differed regarding this verse. The people of Basra read *yukrimūna* and what follows it entirely with the *yā'* (third person), while the others read it with the *tā'* (second person). ﴿And you do not urge one another to feed the needy﴾: Abu Ja'far and the people of Kufa read *tahāḍḍūna* with an *alif* and an open *tā'*. Al-Shadhhari related from al-Kisa'i *tuḥāḍḍūna* with a *ḍammah* on the *tā'*. Others read *taḥuḍḍūna* without the *alif*. ﴿And you devour the inheritance greedily﴾: *al-turāth* is the inheritance, and *aklan lamman* means intense, excessive eating. Al-Hasan said: he eats his own share and the share of others. Bakr ibn 'Abd Allah said: *al-lamm* is transgression in inheritance; he consumes his own inheritance and that of others. Ibn Zayd said: *al-akl al-lamm* is the eating of one who devours everything he finds without asking whether it is lawful or unlawful, consuming what is his and what belongs to others. This was because they did not give inheritance to women or children. [The verse] ﴿They ask you concerning women. Say: Allah gives you a ruling concerning them﴾ and so on was recited. Abu 'Ubayda said: it is said, *lammtu mā 'alā al-khiwān* (I licked up what was on the tray), when one reaches what is on it and eats it all together.

﴿And you love wealth with an abundant love﴾: *jamman* means much, abundant. It is said *jamma al-mā' fī al-ḥawḍ* (the water gathered in the basin) when it became abundant and collected. ﴿No!﴾ This is not how the matter ought to be. Then He informed about those who lament over what they have passed by, when it will no longer benefit them, saying, exalted is He who speaks:

﴿When the earth is pounded to powder, powder upon powder﴾: meaning, repeatedly, time after time, so that everything upon it is crushed.

﴿And your Lord comes﴾: al-Hasan said: His command and His judgment. The people of spiritual allusion (*ahl al-ishārah*) said: the manifestation of your Lord's power. Matters are settled, and the Truth cannot be described as moving from place to place; how could He move about or travel, when He has no place or time, and no moment or duration applies to Him? For to be deprived of a moment regarding something means to miss the moments, and whoever misses something is incapable, whereas the Truth is far above having His attributes contained by natures or encompassed by hearts.

﴿And the angels come in ranks, rank upon rank, and on that Day Hell is brought near﴾.

Ibn Fanjawayh informed me, saying: Ibn Majah told us, saying: Ya'qub ibn Yusuf al-Qarawi told us, saying: al-Qasim ibn al-Hakam told us, saying: 'Ubayd Allah ibn al-Walid told us, saying: 'Atiyyah told us, from Abu Sa'id, who said: When this verse was revealed, ﴿And on that Day Hell is brought near﴾, the color of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) changed and sweat appeared on his face, to the extent that what his companions saw of his condition weighed heavily upon them. Some of them went to 'Ali (may Allah be pleased with him) and said: "O 'Ali, something has happened which we have seen in the Prophet of Allah (ﷺ)." So 'Ali came, embraced him from behind, kissed between his shoulders, and said: "O Prophet of Allah, may my father and mother be your ransom, what has happened today and what has changed you?"

He said: "Jibril (peace be upon him) came and recited to me this verse: ﴿No! When the earth is pounded to powder, powder upon powder, and your Lord comes, and the angels in ranks, rank upon rank, and on that Day Hell is brought near.﴾" I said: "How will it be brought?" He said: "Seventy thousand angels will bring it, leading it by seventy thousand bridles, and it will break loose with such a plunge that if it were left it would burn the people of the gathering. Then Hell will confront me and say: 'What is between me and you, O Muhammad? Allah has forbidden your flesh and blood to me.' No one will remain except that he says: 'myself, myself,' while Muhammad says: 'my nation, my nation.' Then Allah, glory be to Him, will say to the angels: 'Do you not see the people saying: "My Lord, myself, myself," while Muhammad says: "my nation, my nation"?'"[145] [[Tafsir al-Qurtubi: 20/56.]]

Abdullah ibn Mas'ud and Muqatil said regarding this verse: Hell will be led by seventy thousand *zamān* (chains or bridles), each bridle in the hand of seventy thousand angels; it will roar and groan until it is placed on the left of the Throne.

﴿On that Day man will remember, but how will the reminder benefit him?﴾ ﴿He will say: "Would that I had sent ahead for my life"﴾, that is, for my life in the Hereafter. ﴿On that Day none will punish as He punishes, and none will bind as He binds.﴾ The majority read it with a *kasrah* on the *dhāl* and the *thā'* (*yu'adhdhibu* and *yūthiqu*), meaning: no one in this world punishes like Allah's punishment on that Day.

Al-Farra' said: it was also said that this refers to a specific man, Umayyah ibn Khalaf al-Jumahi. The meaning is: no one punishes like the punishment of this disbeliever, and no one binds like his binding. Abu 'Ubayd and Abu Hatim preferred this recitation, because:

Muhammad ibn Nu'aym informed us, saying: al-Husayn ibn Ayyub informed us, saying: 'Ali ibn 'Abd al-'Aziz informed us, saying: al-Qasim ibn Sallam informed us, saying: Hushaym and 'Abbad ibn 'Abbad told us, from Khalid al-Hadhdha', from Abu Qilabah, from one whom the Prophet (ﷺ) had taught to recite, *fa-yawma'idhin lā yu'adhdhabu 'adhābahu aḥadun wa lā yūthaqu wathāqahu aḥad*, with the *dhāl* and *thā'* pronounced with a *fatḥah*.

It is also related that Abu 'Amr returned in the last part of his life to the recitation of the Prophet (ﷺ).

The meaning of the verse is: no one among creation reaches the extent of Allah's punishment and binding, and that is the reference to the chains and the shackles.

Ibn Fanjawayh informed us, saying: Ibn Malik told us, saying: Ibn Hanbal told us, saying: my father told me, saying:

Muhammad ibn Ja'far told us, saying: Shu'bah told us, from Khalid al-Hadhdha', from Abu Qilabah, from one who heard the Prophet (ﷺ) recite *fa-yawma'idhin lā yu'adhdhibu 'adhābahu aḥadun wa lā yūthiqu wathāqahu aḥad*, meaning: "no one does to him."

﴿O soul at rest﴾, content with what Allah has promised, confirming what He has said.

Mujahid said: *al-munība* is the humble and submissive one who has become certain that Allah, glory be to Him, is our Lord, and who has steeled her heart for His command.

Al-Musayyib said: I heard al-Kalbi and Abu Rawq say: it is the one whose face Allah whitens, and to whom He gives her book in her right hand; then at that moment she is at rest. Al-Hasan said: the believing and certain one. 'Atiyyah said: the one content with Allah's decree. Hayyan, from al-Kalbi: the one safe from the punishment of Allah, exalted is He.[[Tafsir al-Tabari: 30/238.]]
